records.title: Vikram and the Corpse-Demon Betal
records.summary: Set in ancient Ujjain, King Vikramaditya is tasked by a deceitful ascetic to retrieve a corpse suspended from a cremation tree, only to discover it is inhabited by the riddle-posing spirit Betal. On the journey back to the cemetery, Betal recounts intricate ethical and moral dilemmas regarding kingship, kinship, and justice. Should the king answer correctly, the demon flees back to the tree; should he remain silent while knowing the truth, his head will burst. The frame narrative tests royal wisdom, persistence, and discernment under spectral duress.
records.historical_period: Ancient Sanskrit Era (c. 11th Century CE Kathasaritsagara compilation)

records.title: The Brahmin and the Loyal Mongoose
records.summary: In this foundational Panchatantra fable, a poor Brahmin and his wife raise a young mongoose alongside their newborn son as an adoptive sibling. When the mother departs to draw river water, a venomous black cobra slithers near the cradle. The faithful mongoose battles and slays the snake to protect the child. Returning home, the mother sees blood on the creature's muzzle and, leaping to the hasty conclusion that it has harmed her infant, strikes it dead with her heavy water pot, only to find her baby sleeping peacefully beside the serpent's carcass.
records.historical_period: Classical India (c. 300 BCE Vishnu Sharma Panchatantra)

records.title: The Monkey and the Crocodile
records.summary: A fruit-eating monkey dwelling in a rose-apple tree on the riverbank befriends a crocodile, frequently sharing sweet berries with him. The crocodile's envious wife demands the monkey's heart, claiming it must be as sweet as the fruit he consumes. Lured into the river under the pretext of hospitality, the monkey discovers the deception midway across. Thinking swiftly, he convinces the predator that monkeys store their hearts hanging safely in tree branches. Upon returning to shore to fetch it, the monkey leaps to freedom, demonstrating that presence of mind overcomes brute strength.
records.historical_period: Ancient Buddhist Era (c. 3rd Century BCE Jataka Tales)
community_attributions: Early Buddhist and Jataka narrative schools

records.title: The Devotion of Savitri and Satyavan
records.summary: Princess Savitri chooses to marry Satyavan, an impoverished prince living in exile, despite Sage Narada's warning that he is destined to die within a year. When the appointed day arrives in the dense forest, Yama, the god of death, arrives to claim Satyavan's departing soul. Savitri relentlessly follows the dark divinity into the spiritual realm. Moved by her unwavering devotion, philosophical discourse, and virtuous argumentation, Yama grants her successive boons, culminating in the restoration of her husband's life and the reclamation of his lost royal kingdom.
records.historical_period: Epic Period (c. 400 BCE Mahabharata, Vana Parva)
records.region_or_community: Salwa and Madra Kingdoms, Northern India

records.title: Tenali Rama and the Well-Water Thieves
records.summary: Noticing suspicious prowlers lurking near his residence at nightfall, court jester Tenali Rama loudly informs his wife that they must safeguard their heavy brass box of jewels from thieves by dropping it into the garden well. Rama fills an iron trunk with heavy paving stones and hurls it into the deep water with an echoing splash. The eavesdropping thieves spend the entire night drawing bucket after bucket from the well to drain it and reach the sunken treasure, unknowingly irrigating Rama's parched vegetable plantation before fleeing empty-handed at daybreak.
records.historical_period: Vijayanagara Empire (c. 16th Century CE, Reign of Krishnadevaraya)

records.title: The Clever Hare and the Tyrant Lion
records.summary: A fierce lion named Bhasuraka terrorizes a jungle kingdom, indiscriminately slaughtering creatures until the forest animals negotiate a pact: one animal will voluntarily present itself daily for his meal. When the turn falls to a diminutive hare, he deliberately arrives late, claiming that another mighty lion detained him and claimed supreme dominion over the woods. Enraged, Bhasuraka demands to see this rival. The hare leads him to a deep stone well; seeing his own fierce reflection and hearing his amplified roar in the water below, the lion leaps into the abyss and perishes.
records.historical_period: Ancient Classical Era (c. 300 BCE Hitopadesha and Panchatantra)

records.title: The Demon and the Boastful Potter
records.summary: During a torrential monsoon night, an old village potter who has imbibed country liquor mistakes a fearsome tiger sheltering near his hut for his wayward donkey. He beats the predator with a stick and rides it into town, while the bewildered beast believes it has fallen into the clutches of a dreaded legendary monster known as 'Drip-Drip' (the leaking ceiling). When a forest demon approaches the tiger to inquire about its humility, the potter's quick-witted bluffs terrify both supernatural predators into abandoning the region forever.
alternate_names: The Tiger, the Brahman, and the Jackal

records.title: The Trials of King Harishchandra
records.summary: Renowned across the heavens for his unyielding adherence to truth, King Harishchandra of Ayodhya is subjected to agonizing tests by Sage Vishvamitra. The king surrenders his entire realm, wealth, and crown, and is forced to sell his queen and son into servitude before binding himself as an assistant to a cremation ground keeper at Kashi. When his son dies of snakebite and his destitute queen brings the corpse for burning, Harishchandra refuses to waive the mandatory cremation toll without payment, upholding righteousness until the deities intervene to restore his realm.

records.title: The Legend of Shakuntala and the Lost Signet Ring
records.summary: Raised in the idyllic forest hermitage of Sage Kanva, Shakuntala falls in love with King Dushyanta during his royal hunt, and the pair marry in Gandharva rites. Upon departing for his capital, the monarch bestows his royal signet ring as a token of pledge. Lost in reverie, Shakuntala inadvertently neglects hospitality toward the volatile sage Durvasa, who curses her: the one she yearns for will forget her entirely until shown the token. While bathing in a sacred river, she loses the ring to a fish, triggering heartbreak and exile before redemption.

records.title: The Golden Deer of Panchavati
records.summary: During their forest exile at Panchavati along the Godavari River, Sita catches sight of a dazzling golden deer with sapphire-tipped antlers grazing among the trees, unaware that it is the sorcerer Maricha transformed through demonic illusion. Captivated by its ethereal radiance, Sita pleads with Rama to capture the creature. When Rama pierces the fleeing phantom with a golden arrow, the dying sorcerer mimics Rama's distressed voice to call for Lakshmana, drawing away the protector and leaving the forest dwelling exposed to abduction.
alternate_names: The Illusion of the Golden Deer
